title: Salary Spread by Department Using STDDEV_POP
description:
Calculate the population standard deviation and average salary for each department to understand how spread out salaries are.

**Table: employees** — `id`, `name`, `department`, `salary`

Output columns: `department`, `avg_salary`, `salary_stddev`, `headcount`. Order by `department`.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR, department VARCHAR, salary INT); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Alice','Engineering',95000),(2,'Bob','Engineering',88000),(3,'Carol','Engineering',92000),(4,'Dave','Engineering',110000),(5,'Eve','Engineering',85000),(6,'Frank','Marketing',72000),(7,'Grace','Marketing',68000),(8,'Henry','Marketing',75000),(9,'Iris','HR',58000),(10,'Jake','HR',62000),(11,'Kim','HR',55000);
solution_sql: SELECT department, ROUND(AVG(salary), 0) AS avg_salary, ROUND(STDDEV_POP(salary), 2) AS salary_stddev, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY department

test_cases.description: 3 departments; Engineering has the highest salary spread (stddev); HR the lowest

hints: STDDEV_POP computes the population standard deviation (divides by N); use STDDEV_SAMP to divide by N-1 for a sample.
A high stddev relative to avg indicates a wide salary range within the department.
explanation: STDDEV_POP(salary) measures dispersion around the mean. Engineering: avg=94000, values span 85k-110k → higher stddev. Marketing: avg≈71667, values span 68k-75k → lower stddev. HR: avg≈58333, span 55k-62k → lowest stddev. High stddev relative to average indicates large pay variation, which matters for equity analysis.
